extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent attorneys/agents, and patent drafters (esp. software and biotech practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical drafting guidance for patent claims and specifications to align with recurring Federal Circuit case law and avoid pitfalls in prosecution and litigation. Focuses on claim construction, 35 U.S.C. §112 issues, subject-matter eligibility, continuation practice, and inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Lexicography Beats Claim Construction Surprises
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit repeatedly defers to explicit definitions in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: For any claim term whose ordinary meaning may not capture your intended scope, define it explicitly. Use clear definitional language such as 'As used herein, X means Y.' Relying on explicit spec lexicography reduces the risk of unexpected claim constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers Must Be Clear and Unmistakable
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements in the specification or during prosecution can disclaim claim scope only if they are clear and unmistakable; vague characterizations of prior art are usually not disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of disclaimers: statements like 'the invention requires X' or 'in contrast to prior art Y, the invention does not include Y' can operate as disclaimers. Drafting implication: avoid language that could be read as an explicit disclaimer of claim scope; be cautious in characterizing prior art or describing preferred embodiments so as not to unintentionally narrow claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method Claims Need Single-Actor Architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct infringement of a method claim by multiple actors requires proof of direction or control or a joint enterprise (Akamai line of cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: where possible, draft method claims so that a single actor performs all steps. If multiple actors are unavoidable, structure the claims or the specification to show one party directing/controlling the others (e.g., through instruction, contractual relationship, or agent/principal language) to support liability for divided performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Language Without Structure Triggers 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms like 'module configured to,' 'mechanism for,' 'system that performs' without structural anchoring may be construed as means-plus-function under 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (Williamson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: Use concrete structural terminology (processor, circuit, memory, sensor, database, etc.) and supply corresponding structure in the specification to avoid §112(f) treatment. When using functional phrasing, provide clear structural examples or algorithms in the spec as corresponding structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Survives With Concrete Technical Improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice, claims are more likely patent-eligible when they recite specific technical mechanisms tied to a concrete improvement in computer functioning (cases such as Enfish, McRO, Visual Memory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: For software-related inventions, anchor the specification and claims in a specific technical improvement (e.g., reduced latency, improved memory utilization, a novel data structure, enhanced signal processing), rather than framing the invention as merely solving a business problem or performing generic computer tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description for Genus Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus claims in unpredictable arts (e.g., biotechnology, chemistry), Amgen v. Sanofi and Ariad require disclosure of representative species and a unifying structure or common feature to satisfy written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: Disclose multiple representative species and identify the common structural or functional features that unify the genus. Provide examples, experimental results, or other evidence showing possession of the claimed genus across embodiments to support broad claims in unpredictable fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Limitations Need Spec Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative claim limitations (for example, 'wherein the device is free of X') require explicit specification support that the excluded feature is or may be omitted (Santarus v. Par).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: If you intend to claim the absence of a feature, explicitly state in the specification that the feature can be omitted and describe embodiments or rationale for excluding it; do not rely on mere silence or implication to support negative limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range Claims Need Range Disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed ranges should be supported by specification disclosure of the range or at least the endpoints (In re Wertheim and progeny).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: Disclose multiple ranges and endpoints in the specification, and provide examples or data where appropriate to support claimed numerical ranges. Consider describing preferred sub-ranges and how endpoints were chosen to reduce indefiniteness or lack-of-support issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation Practice Requires Pendency
rubrics_metrics.description: To file a continuation application, the parent application must be pending at the time the continuation is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: Calendar the parent's issue fee, abandonment, and terminal dates; decide before the parent issues whether to file continuations or plan to file a request to extend/contest allowance. Manage prosecution timelines proactively to preserve continuation options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship Errors Are Curable but Risky
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventorship errors can be corrected under 35 U.S.C. §256 in the absence of deceptive intent, but correcting inventorship discovered during litigation can be costly and risky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting implication: Conduct inventorship audits at filing, at allowance, and after any substantive amendments to reduce the risk of later disputes. Keep clear inventor documentation and consider pre-suit corrections where appropriate to avoid expensive litigation-stage cures.
